articles.title: Materializing Memory and Myth: Juninho’s Artifacts, Institutional Appropriation, and the Reconfiguration of Post‑war Verdantine Identity
articles.abstract: This article argues that the contested fate of Juninho’s material remains and the competing uses of his image by museums, religious movements, bards, and state institutions were central to the reshaping of Verdantine political and social life after the war. Using archival records, bardic corpora, oral histories, and provenance case studies of key artifacts, it traces how mythmaking and institutional appropriation produced durable but fragmented legacies and how recent scholarship and repatriation debates have reopened those contestations.

sections.name: Introduction: Juninho, Memory, and the Stakes of Materiality
sections.content:
1. Introduction: Juninho, Memory, and the Stakes of Materiality

Juninho is not a single, stable referent in post‑war Verdantine discourse but a composite of embodied fragments—objects, images, texts, and performative acts—whose dispersal and re‑inscription have been central to the reconfiguration of Verdantine political culture and social life. This article concentrates on a narrowly defined but theoretically consequential phenomenon: the materialization of Juninho’s memory through contested artifacts and the institutional strategies that sought to appropriate, authenticate, and instrumentalize those artifacts in the decades after the war. Rather than treating mythmaking and institutional appropriation as parallel or equivalent processes, I argue that the interplay between the two—how institutions (museums, state archives, religious movements) engaged with, transformed, and sometimes suppressed vernacular mediations (bardic performance, household reliquaries, oral histories)—produced durable yet fragmented legacies that shaped new forms of authority, belonging, and dissent in Verdantine society.

The theoretical frame merges recent advances in material culture and memory studies with approaches to heritage politics and post‑conflict identity formation. From the literature on lieux de mémoire and the object biography of things, I draw the premise that artifacts are active mediators of memory: they do not merely symbolize past events but participate in the production of meaning through their material affordances, circulation histories, and institutional contexts. From studies of authorized heritage discourse and cultural property politics, I adopt the claim that institutions enact particular mnemonic regimes—configurations of legitimacy, access, and expertise—that compete with vernacular regimes of remembering (bardic repertoires, household practices, ritual economies). Together, these frameworks direct attention to three interrelated stakes of materiality in the Juninho case: (1) epistemic authority—who gets to determine what counts as authentic Juninho; (2) political legitimacy—how possession or display of Juninho’s artifacts confers moral capital or sovereign claims; and (3) affective efficacy—how objects sustain ritual, performative, and therapeutic practices that connect communities to contested pasts.

Empirically, the paper centers on a set of provenance case studies—most notably the so‑called sword, cloak, and hymnbook attributed to Juninho—traced through museum accession records, wartime cartography, bardic corpora, and oral histories collected in both rural and urban Verdantine localities. These cases are chosen not because they exhaust Juninho’s material traces but because they exemplify recurring dynamics: fragmentation of artifacts during wartime displacement; multiple, overlapping chains of custody (household, religious congregation, state archive, private collectors); differential regimes of authentication (expert conservation reports, bardic attributions, ecclesiastical validation); and episodic legal and extra‑legal contests over ownership and display. Methodologically, I combine close provenance reconstruction—archival triangulation of acquisition files, correspondence, and accession logs—with textual analysis of bardic versions of Juninho narratives and ethnographic readings of contemporary ritual uses. This mixed method foregrounds both documental evidence and living practices, enabling a granular account of how objects moved between meanings and institutions.

The argument unfolds in three propositions. First, the material dispersal of Juninho’s remains produced a plural field of memory in which authenticity was multiply instituted: museums sought to stabilize Juninho as a national exemplar through curated display and archival cataloguing; religious movements reframed fragments as relics that conferred spiritual authority and ritual efficacy; bardic communities sustained vernacular genealogies that prioritized performative continuity over curatorial provenance. These competing forms of authentication were not merely contestatory but often symbiotic—museums incorporated bardic narratives into exhibitions, and religious movements engaged in formal petitions to state repositories—resulting in hybrid mnemonic practices that complicated simple binaries of elite versus vernacular memory.

Second, institutional appropriation of Juninho’s materiality was integral to state‑building and the remaking of Verdantine identity. In the immediate post‑war period, state actors instrumentalized select artifacts and iconographies to legitimate new political projects: national museums performed rituals of consolidation by integrating Juninho into official iconography; commemorative legislation codified certain narratives while silencing others; archival classifications insulated state claims to custody. These processes demonstrate how material culture operates as both instrument and terrain of political contestation, shaping access to moral capital and discourses of rightful inheritance in ways that outlast immediate post‑conflict stabilization.

Third, the re‑emergence of contested provenance claims and repatriation debates in recent decades has reopened fractures rather than resolving them. Scholarly interventions—critical provenance studies, renewed oral history projects, and publication of bardic corpora—have destabilized institutional narratives and facilitated grassroots demands for restitution and reinterpretation. Yet these debates also reveal the limits of legalistic or restitutional frameworks when objects simultaneously function as liturgical relics, performance props, and museum specimens; resolving one dimension of ownership can intensify claims along another.

This section sets out the stakes and scope of the study: it foregrounds materiality as a productive lens for understanding how memory, myth, and institutional power interlock in post‑war Verdantine society. The following section outlines the archival and fieldwork corpus and the analytic procedures used for provenance reconstruction. Subsequent sections trace (a) institutional strategies of appropriation and display, (b) vernacular performative continuities mediated by bardic practice, and (c) the contemporary repatriation controversies and their implications for Verdantine identity politics. By anchoring debate about Juninho in the contingent trajectories of things, the article contributes to broader conversations on how objects mediate post‑conflict memory, how institutional authority is materially produced, and how contested legacies can remain both embodied and contested across generations.

sections.name: Sources and Analytical Framework: Archives, Bardic Texts, Oral Histories, and Provenance Research
sections.content:
2. Sources and Analytical Framework: Archives, Bardic Texts, Oral Histories, and Provenance Research

This section sets out the empirical base and interpretive instruments used to trace how Juninho’s physical remains and representational image were mobilized across competing institutional arenas after the war. The argument requires reconstructing intersecting trajectories — of objects, texts, performances, and institutional practices — so the methodology combines (a) traditional archival criticism, (b) corpus and performance-oriented analysis of bardic materials, (c) systematic oral-history collection and evaluation, and (d) forensic and documentary provenance research. These strands are deployed in a deliberately convergent design: each source type is read against the others to expose silences, displacements, and acts of appropriation that produced the Verdantine post‑war mnemonic field.

1. Source types and selection criteria
- Material artifacts: items explicitly ascribed to Juninho in institutional records or bardic repertoire (e.g., garments, ritual objects, fragments), plus paraphernalia used in post‑war commemorative practices. Selection prioritizes objects with extant accession or acquisition documentation, known chains of custody, or recurring presence in bardic/ritual texts.
- Archival records: museum accession ledgers, acquisition correspondence, colonial and postwar administrative files, exhibition catalogs, clerical registers of religious orders, police and military reports on dispersal of remains, auction house catalogs, and private collection inventories. Emphasis on primary documentation that documents transfer, deaccession, loan, or display.
- Bardic corpus: transcribed songs, heroic lays, epitaphic chants, and performative scripts circulated in bardic guilds or recorded in oral-literary collections. Both published anthologies and field transcripts are included, with attention to variant forms across time and locale.
- Oral histories: interviews with surviving bards, ritual specialists, museum staff (curators, registrars), clergy, collectors, and community members involved in post‑war commemorative practices. Prioritize informants who participated directly in transfers, displays, or claim-making.
- Scientific and conservation reports: condition reports, conservation treatment records, XRF/EDX, radiocarbon or dendrochronological data when available, and photographic/CT imaging that bear on material authenticity and history of use.

Selection is bounded chronologically to the immediate post‑war decades (the “formative” period of Verdantine memory politics) while remaining attentive to later acts of re‑appropriation (e.g., 1990s–present repatriation debates). Geographically, the inquiry focuses on Verdantine institutions and transnational repositories known to have received material from the conflict zone.

2. Archival criticism and institutional record analysis
Archival work proceeds under principles of provenance and fonds integrity: documents are analyzed within their originating administrative contexts to avoid anachronistic reclassification that can mask institutional agendas (the archival concept of fonds and series is applied). Special attention is paid to:
- Acquisition and accession records: dates, donor statements, conditions of gift, accession numbers, and any registration anomalies.
- Correspondence and memoranda: letters between museums, religious orders, collectors, and state apparatus that reveal intent, negotiation, and ideology behind transfers.
- Exhibition and interpretive texts: catalog entries and labels are treated as active constructors of meaning, producing institutional narratives that appropriate Juninho’s image.
- Archival silences and absences: following the politics-of‑knowledge critique (cf. archival silences), gaps are treated as evidence of contested control, intentional omission, or legal/ethical avoidance.

Methodologically, records are coded for actors, actions (acquisition, display, deaccession, loan), stated rationales (scientific, devotional, nationalist, pedagogic), and legal instruments (permits, export papers). Provenance inconsistencies are flagged for targeted material analysis.

3. Bardic texts: corpus construction and performance analysis
The bardic corpus is both textual and performative; analytic methods are adapted from oral‑formulaic studies and performance theory. Key tools include:
- Variant mapping: constructing a diachronic register of textual variants of Juninho-related lays to trace when and how motifs (martyrdom, sanctity, defilement, heroics) enter institutional narratives.
- Prosodic and mnemonic analysis: identifying formulaic structures, refrains, and performative devices that stabilize or destabilize claims about Juninho’s personhood (drawing on oral‑formulaic theory).
- Ethnopoetic transcription: preserving performance features (intonation, pause, audience interaction) where recordings exist, since these features contribute to authority and authenticity claims.
- Intertextual reading: comparing bardic versions with museum narratives and religious liturgies to identify appropriation, selective citation, or silencing of particular motifs.

Bardic authority — the social standing of bards as claimants to authentic memory — is operationalized as a variable: variations in a bard’s claim to Juninho’s narrative are traced against institutional endorsements (e.g., invitations to perform at museum openings) that convert oral authority into institutional legitimacy.

4. Oral histories: protocol and interpretive precautions
Oral testimony is central to reconstructing transfers and meanings that are absent or obscured in institutional records, but it requires explicit methodological controls:
- Sampling and triangulation: purposive sampling targets interlocutors with direct knowledge of events; triangulation uses independent testimony, archival records, and material evidence to confirm or contest accounts.
- Interview technique: semi‑structured interviews elicit narrative sequences, recollection of transactions, and personal assessments of Juninho’s symbolic value. Life‑history prompts situate informants’ memories within broader mnemonic regimes.
- Memory politics and social desirability: caution is taken with retrospective reconstruction and with the influence of contemporary repatriation debates on recollection; corroboratory prompts and cross-referencing reduce uncritical reliance on single narratives.
- Translation and transcription: linguistic nuances relevant to vernacular idioms for sanctity and heroism are preserved; where translation is necessary, glosses retain culturally loaded terms that shape meaning.

Ethical practice includes informed consent, community consultation in the interpretation of sensitive material, and attention to the potential impact of disclosures on ongoing restitution claims.

5. Provenance research and material analysis
Provenance research integrates documentary chains of custody with scientific methods and the “object biography” approach (treating artifacts as actors with entangled histories). Steps include:
- Documentary chain reconstruction: sequentially establish transfers via accession ledgers, donor correspondence, export/import permits, customs records, and auction catalogs.
- Physical-tag and label archaeology: examine labelling practices, collection stamps, and past condition reports to recover short‑term custodial histories often unrecorded in formal archives.
- Scientific authentication: where contested, apply non‑destructive analytical techniques (XRF elemental analysis, FTIR, microscopy) and, when ethically and legally permissible, invasive dating methods (radiocarbon, dendrochronology). Conservation reports help identify restorations that might signify re‑fashioning for display or marketability.
- Comparative material culture: situate Juninho items against typologies of Verdantine material culture (materials, manufacture techniques) to identify anachronism, regional provenance, or workshop markers that corroborate or undermine claims.
- Legal and transactional documents: study permits, deeds of gift, purchase receipts, and international conventions invoked during dispersals (e.g., export licenses, 1970 UNESCO treaty analogues) to map legal rationales for transfers.

Provenance research is iterative: material findings prompt targeted archival searches; documentary anomalies prompt specific tests. The aim is not only authentication but to reveal the institutional logics that authorized appropriation.

6. Integrative analytical frame
Four interpretive lenses structure analysis across sources:
- Mnemonic institutions: how museums, religious bodies, and state agencies institutionalize memory through practices of collection, display, liturgy, and commemoration (drawing on work on lieux de mémoire and institutional memory).
- Performativity and authority: how bardic performance and ritual enactment generate and contest authority over Juninho’s legacy (deploying concepts from performance studies and oral‑formulaic theory).
- Provenancial politics: how ownership, legality, and market forces mediate the mobility and meaning of Juninho’s artifacts (combining provenance studies, object biography, and material culture theory).
- Postcolonial and settler‑state critique: how power asymmetries shape whose version of Juninho becomes public property, and how repatriation debates renegotiate sovereignty over memory (methods from postcolonial museum studies and critical heritage studies).

Operationally, the article employs comparative case studies of key artifacts as nodes where these lenses intersect. Each case study pairs: (i) the archival dossier (accession, correspondence, display history), (ii) the bardic textual record and performance variants tied to that object, (iii) oral testimony from stakeholders, and (iv) material/scientific analysis. Cross‑case comparison surfaces patterns of institutional appropriation and the fragmentation of legacy.

7. Digital and quantitative adjuncts
To manage variant-rich corpora and provenance chains the project uses:
- A relational database to connect actors, objects, documents, and performance instances (fields for dates, accession numbers, provenance notes, informant IDs).
- Text‑encoding (TEI) for bardic variants to enable computational collation and motif‑tracking.
- Network analysis to visualize institutional linkages (museums, religious orders, collectors) and the flows of objects and narratives.
- GIS mapping of object movements and performance loci to spatialize appropriation trajectories.

8. Limitations, biases, and ethical constraints
- Archival incompleteness and deliberate obfuscation limit certainty; where evidence is fragmentary, claims are qualified and framed as probabilistic reconstructions.
- Scientific testing is contingent on access and legal permission; in many cases non‑destructive analysis is the only option.
- Oral testimony is subject to retrospective reshaping by contemporary debates; triangulation mitigates, but does not eliminate, this risk.
- Community sensitivities and ongoing repatriation claims require foregrounding consultative protocols; some archives or objects may be deliberately inaccessible.

Conclusion and how this framework advances the article
By combining rigorous archival criticism, performance‑attentive reading of bardic texts, ethically grounded oral history, and forensic provenance work within an integrative mnemonic‑institutional frame, the article reconstructs not merely the biography of objects but the processes through which Juninho’s materiality was instrumentalized. This methodological synthesis permits explanation of enduring fragmentation in Verdantine memory — why multiple, competing legacies cohere within particular institutions while others are effaced — and grounds subsequent case studies in demonstrable chains of action, meaning‑making, and institutional motive.

sections.name: Competing Narrative Brokers: Museums, Religious Movements, Political Institutions, and Bards
sections.content:
3. Competing Narrative Brokers: Museums, Religious Movements, Political Institutions, and Bards

This section maps how four distinct sets of narrative brokers—museums, religious movements, political institutions, and bards—contested Juninho’s materiality and image in the post‑war period, and how their differing epistemic claims and material practices recomposed Verdantine social and political identities. Drawing on provenance dossiers, accession ledgers, archival correspondence, bardic corpora, and oral histories, I isolate the mechanisms through which each broker produced authoritative versions of Juninho’s life and death, and analyze the points of friction where these versions collided. The analysis centers on the shared political economy of relics and representations—what I term the authority of materiality—and on how institutional formality, ritual practice, state power, and vernacular performance generated overlapping but non‑congruent legacies.

1. Museums: institutionalization, display regimes, and the politics of authentication
Post‑war museums in Verdantine acted as primary vehicles for transforming Juninho from historical actor into a museum object—an operation that involved cataloging, conservation, contextualization, and selective omission. Museums deployed provenance narratives and display logics that naturalized particular teleologies: heroism, national rebirth, or reconciliation. Archival accessions indicate three recurrent museum tactics:

- Canonization through typology: Museums framed Juninho’s artifacts (garments, personal equipment, a battle standard, and fragments of purported remains) within typologies that linked them to pre‑existing national narratives—military valor, civic sacrifice, or victimhood—thus embedding them within institutional genealogies of state formation.
- Technical authentication as authority: Institutions foregrounded laboratory reports, conservation histories, and provenance chains to claim epistemic superiority. Reference to isotopic analyses, textile conservation notes, or curator’s acquisition memos served to close debate by recoding contested objects as scientifically validated evidence of Juninho’s historicity.
- Spatialized memory: Exhibition design—placement in national halls versus regional galleries, juxtaposition with other artifacts, and interpretive labels—controlled interpretive frames. Museums that emphasized reconciliation placed Juninho among civilian casualties and cultural losses; those aligned with state narratives isolated heroic episodes and minimized ambivalence.

The effect of museum practice was to produce a stabilized, commodified Juninho for publics who encounter him in routinized institutional contexts. However, empirical provenance case studies reveal frequent discontinuities: accession records showing unverified donations, anonymized intermediaries, and gaps in chain‑of‑custody—weaknesses that other brokers exploited.

2. Religious movements: sacralization, relic cults, and the politics of devotion
Religious movements responded to Juninho’s material traces by reconfiguring them as sacral objects. Where museums rendered artifacts as historical evidence, religious actors re‑sacralized them—transforming battle cloths, fragments of bone, and personal items into relics invested with talismanic potency. Four distinctive practices are notable in the records:

- Relicization and liturgical incorporation: Artifacts became incorporated into devotional objects and rites—processions, blessings, and miracle narratives—producing affective economies distinct from museums’ didacticism.
- Charismatic authentication: Rather than scientific verification, authentication occurred through claims of miraculous efficacy, testimony of healings, or endorsement by charismatic leaders. Oral histories document local miracles associated with Juninho’s sash and contested bone fragments.
- Pilgrimage and spatial claims: Religious appropriation produced pilgrimage circuits around sites where Juninho’s purported artifacts were enshrined, generating grassroots forms of memory economy and territorial claims that sometimes contradicted state narratives.
- Syncretic politics: Religious actors selectively integrated Juninho into pre‑existing cosmologies, effacing political dimensions of his life by emphasizing moral exemplarity or sanctity; alternatively, some movements used sacralization to political ends, endorsing contemporary agendas under the guise of devotion.

Religious appropriation bypassed museum epistemologies and appealed directly to embodied, experiential claims—forming counter‑archives grounded in testimony and ritual efficacy. These rival claims challenged institutional attempts to monopolize Juninho’s material authority.

3. Political institutions: emblematic uses, legitimacy claims, and legal maneuvers
State and partisan institutions instrumentalized Juninho’s image to serve regimes of legitimacy and governance. Political actors employed three interlocking strategies:

- Symbolic appropriation and nationalist mythmaking: Juninho’s image was instrumented to authorize new constitutional narratives, public ceremonies, and state anniversaries. Iconography derived from museum displays and official biographies was disseminated in public schools, monuments, and media campaigns to naturalize particular readings of the war and of state continuity.
- Legal and bureaucratic control of artifacts: Ministries of culture and heritage legislated ownership, regulated access, and mediated repatriation claims through legal frameworks—often privileging national custody over local or religious claims. Archival correspondence shows litigation over possession of key objects and state decrees that designated certain artifacts as “national patrimony.”
- Strategic silence and selective memory: Political institutions occasionally practiced omission—deliberately excluding inconvenient aspects of Juninho’s history (alleged dissidence, internecine violence) to stabilize consensual narratives. Such silences were as constitutive of identity as public commemoration.

Political brokerage thus combined coercive-legal instruments with discursive deployment to incorporate Juninho as a legitimating figure, but institutional efforts often foundered on competing claims of authenticity and on the resonance of local devotional and bardic networks.

4. Bards: vernacular custodianship, performative contestation, and narrative plurality
Bards functioned as vital vernacular brokers whose oral repertoires mediated between official forms and popular memory. Their interactions with Juninho’s material traces exhibit several distinctive features:

- Performativity and variant logics: Bardic transmission privileged narrative variability, mnemonic devices, and affective retellings over documentary closure. Bards reproduced, adapted, and contested official narratives, often preserving marginal or oppositional memories absent from museum and state accounts.
- Material engagement and provenance knowledge: Bards served as custodians of localized objects—cloths, songs inscribed on paper relics, orally transmitted details about the location of artifacts—generating an informal provenance knowledge that frequently contradicted institutional chains.
- Legitimacy through practice: The bardic authority rested on communal recognition, performative competence, and intergenerational transmission rather than on legal or scientific validation. Oral histories document how bardic repertoires became flashpoints for mobilization, with songs and narratives used in protest, remembrance, and identity formation.
- Translation between registers: Bards translated ritual claims into narrative form and vice versa, enabling religious groups to adopt songs for processions and allowing political actors to appropriate popular refrains for campaigns.

The bardic domain thus retained a dynamic, contested archive—mobile, adaptive, and often resistant to institutional capture.

5. Intersections, contestations, and the reconfiguration of Verdantine identity
The interaction among these brokers produced recurring patterns: institutional consolidation efforts (museumization and legal control) repeatedly encountered processes of sacralization, vernacular contestation, and claims grounded in lived practice. Three analytical outcomes are noteworthy:

- Fragmentation and pluralization of memory: Rather than converging on a single authoritative Juninho, the coexistence of museum, religious, political, and bardic narratives produced a proliferating field of partial, sometimes contradictory legacies. This fragmentation enabled multiple, simultaneous identities—state citizen, sanctified martyr, regional hero, or subversive icon—each mobilized in different social contexts.
- Materiality as contested capital: Artifacts functioned as forms of cultural capital whose value depended on brokerage. Provenance gaps and contested custody allowed actors with differing legitimacies (charismatic priests, local bards, state curators) to claim authority, turning objects into focal nodes of political struggle.
- Reopening through repatriation and scholarly critique: Recent repatriation claims, forensic re‑examinations, and historiographic critiques have reopened contestations over Juninho’s materiality. Debates over restitution, archival access, and interpretive pluralism challenge prior practices of canonical closure and demand more dialogic models of custody and display.

In sum, the contest among museums, religious movements, political institutions, and bards over Juninho’s artifacts did not merely reflect divergent interpretations; it actively reconfigured Verdantine social relations by remaking the terms of memory, sacrality, and legitimacy. The ensuing section turns to how these negotiated legacies manifest in concrete provenance disputes and repatriation cases, and how those legal‑political processes further reshape public memory.

sections.name: Material Culture and Provenance — Three Case Studies of Juninho’s Artifacts and Their Dispersal
sections.content:
4. Material Culture and Provenance — Three Case Studies of Juninho’s Artifacts and Their Dispersal

Methodological note
This section uses an object-biography approach (sensu Kopytoff; augmented by material-semiotic perspectives such as Gell) combined with provenance reconstruction through archival cross-referencing (military inventories, museum accession records, municipal registries), bardic corpora, oral histories, and recent technical analyses (textile dyeing profiles, metallography, limited biomolecular assays where ethically authorized). The objective is not exhaustive cataloguing but targeted examination of three emblematic artifacts whose divergent trajectories and institutional uses illuminate larger processes of mythmaking, institutional appropriation, and identity reconfiguration in post‑war Verdantine society. Where archival gaps or contested claims exist these are identified and treated as analytic data rather than lacunae to be filled by speculation.

Case study A — The Green Cloak (manta verde)

Object and wartime context
Description: A patchworked woolen cloak predominantly dyed with a distinctive deep-verdant vegetal dye, hemstitched with a frayed silver braid and inscribed in ink with the name Juninho and a short invocation in the vernacular. Measurements (as recorded in 1954 NMV accession file): c. 180 × 120 cm; three large repairs consistent with battlefield wear.

Provenance chain and dispersal
- 1979 edition of the Bardic Cantos of Vale Alto references Juninho “wrapping the green mantle round the wounded,” establishing early symbolic association.
- Contemporary battlefield inventories (1948–1952) list “seragam/vestimenta m. Juninho” as removed by the 3rd Verdantine Infantry. Transfer documented to the local parish (Cathedral of São Lirio) in 1953 under ecclesiastical custody for safekeeping.
- 1967–1974: Cathedral ledger entries indicate the cloak was used as an ex-voto during commemorations; photographic evidence shows communal veneration.
- 1978 Heritage Protection Law institutionalized national custody of “objects of revolutionary provenance”; NMV accession record (1979) reflects legal transfer from Cathedral to National Museum of Verdantine (NMV).
- 1989: A major NMV exhibition “Heroes and Saints” displayed the cloak as a national relic; interpretive label framed Juninho as “martyr and founder.”
- Post-1990s: Fragmentary reproductions circulated in diaspora communities; small textile fragments reportedly given to bardic guilds and a private collector in Lisbon (provenance less well documented).

Materiality and interpretive reuses
The cloak’s textile composition and dye attract two axes of meaning. First, its vegetal dye and mending traces made it a potent index of vernacular material culture and popular sacrifice—amenable to bardic appropriation as a symbol of communal suffering and care. Second, its movement into NMV entailed musealization: conservation practices (deacidification, mounting) stabilized but simultaneously deactivated ritual use. Institutional labels re-framed it within an authorized heritage discourse that privileged national unity, effectively re-coding a locally ritualized object into a state symbol.

Provenance gaps and contention
Key contested intervals: 1953–1979 (parish to museum transfer) drew accusations from local communities that the Cathedral surrendered the cloak under political pressure; the documentary record is partial and mediated by later NMV narratives. The dispersion of small textile fragments (post-1980) generated competing authenticity claims: bardic guilds assert continuity through ritual possession while NMV asserts legal, intact custody. Conservation ethics and repatriation appeals culminated in 2015 negotiations that produced a rotating custody agreement (community display periods within Vale Alto under co-curation terms) — a compromise highlighting both the political value and material constraints of a textile relic.

Implications
The cloak illustrates how a portable, repairable textile becomes a contested memory-technology: its physical vulnerabilities facilitate distribution and multiple localized re-appropriations, while institutional stabilization channels the object into canonical national narratives. The cloak’s dispersal and returned fragments function as markers in the contested terrain between local ritual authority and state heritage regimes.

Case study B — The Serpentine Saber (sabres de serpente)

Object and wartime context
Description: A single‑edged curved saber with a distinctive serpentine engraving on the blade and a hilt inlaid with a small mother-of-pearl disk bearing the maker’s punch of the Luso‑Verdantine craftworks of Porto Verde. Blade length c. 82 cm; microstructural analysis indicates high-phosphorus forging typical of mid-1930s regional manufacture.

Provenance chain and dispersal
- Battlefield testimony (1949–1951 tribunal memos) records the saber as taken from Juninho’s person during the final engagement; military unit report lists it as “war trophy.”
- 1952–1965: The saber was accessioned into the Military History Gallery, stored as part of the Army Museum collection with restricted public access, presented officially as “symbol of victory and reconciliation.”
- 1976 diplomatic gift: Photographic and curator correspondence indicate the saber was gifted by a senior military official to the Altamiran General Staff Museum as a symbol of inter-state rapprochement — a transfer not cleared through heritage law channels.
- 1998: Traced in a private catalog in New Harbor following an estate sale; provenance was asserted by the seller as a “diplomatic transfer” with documentary copies of Altamiran acquisition records.
- 2018–present: Legal challenge initiated under Heritage Protection Law (illicit export clauses) and international norms on cultural property; case currently in arbitration. Forensic metallurgical and punch‑mark matching support the identification as the same blade recorded in wartime inventories.

Materiality and institutionalization
The saber’s solidity and status as a martial object make it a particular instrument of state narrative. Display in military contexts serves to naturalize official versions of the conflict—emphasizing order, professional restoration, and the valorization of armed reconciliation. Contrastingly, bardic and popular traditions repurpose the saber in narrative rhythms that emphasize dispossession and the exile of Juninho’s legacy (“the blade abroad, the name at home”).

Provenance gaps and legal/political stakes
The saber’s transfer to a foreign museum and then into private hands exposes a recurrent mechanism: official actors instrumentalize material gifts to cement diplomatic narratives, while legal/ethical oversight is bypassed. The current litigation foregrounds questions of illicit export, state responsibility for cultural patrimony, and the limits of restorative justice. It also shows how a metal artifact’s durability and portability permit long-distance appropriation, complicating community claims and evidence chains.

Implications
The saber case highlights how material robustness and institutional valorization converge to make some artifacts vehicles of extraterritorial identity claims. Provenance ambiguities generated by diplomatic transfers create legal and interpretive friction; the saber thus became a focus for diasporic mobilization and transnational claims-making around Verdantine memory.

Case study C — The Relic Assemblage (hair lock, blood-stained handkerchief, and communion cloth fragments)

Object and wartime context
Description: A composite set of small biogenic and textile items attributed to Juninho: (a) a short lock of human hair preserved in waxed paper; (b) a small linen handkerchief with hem stained dark brown, described in parish inventories as “bloodied and folded on Juninho’s person”; (c) fragments of a communion cloth reportedly pressed to Juninho’s brow in his death hour.

Provenance chain and dispersal
- Immediate post-mortem: Family testimony and parish registers (1949–1954) describe sequestration of these items by relatives and the Cathedral. Several bardic laments mention the distribution of “small pieces” to kin.
- 1960s–1980s: Relicization by popular Catholic movements and emergent charismatic groups (notably the New Lirio movement) converted these fragments into objects of pilgrimage; vouchers in the Cathedral ledger indicate lending for processions.
- 1994–2004: Small portions entered market circulation—some sold to private collectors, others exhibited in popular-religion displays abroad. Fragmented custodial histories are common; some items exchanged hands informally as tokens among bardic performers.
- 2009–2012: Two small items (lock of hair and a handkerchief fragment) were submitted to an independent laboratory for limited DNA profiling and fiber analysis to establish kinship and textile chronology. Ethical oversight was contested: family consent was partial; the Cathedral denied authorization for testing of liturgical cloth. Results were inconclusive for definitive identification but consistent with a mid-20th-century origin.

Materiality, ritualization, and authentication politics
Biogenic artifacts occupy a different affective register from large artifacts: they intimate bodily presence and are easily divisible, making them ideal for sacral economies of distribution. Their fragmentation enabled multiple localized sacred economies—pilgrimage tokens, bardic amulets, and political talismans serving competing groups. This multiplicity also complicates authentication: small size makes lab analyses possible but contested on ethical grounds (consent, sacred status), and inconclusive results are easily appropriated by competing narratives.

Contestation and repatriation practices
Because custodial contexts included family, ecclesiastical, popular religious organizations, and private collectors, disputes frequently framed itself not as single-return claims but as negotiated sharing. The most visible intervention was the 2013 “Protocol of Shared Safeguarding” negotiated by municipal authorities, family representatives, NMV, and a cathedral committee. The protocol established rotating custody, restrictions on invasive testing, community-curated display rights, and mandated transparent provenance documentation for any future transfers. The protocol has been critiqued by scholars for favoring institutional actors with better legal leverage and by grassroots activists for not fully restituting items seized during early post-war years.

Implications
The relic assemblage exemplifies how small, intimate materials become loci for competing sacral and secular claims. Their easy divisibility allowed for wide dispersal and a proliferation of claims that made exclusive restitution practically and morally fraught. The ethical dilemmas surrounding testing and display foreground the need for protocols that recognize both bodily connection and community agency.

Comparative synthesis and interpretive implications
Three patterns emerge from these case studies, each bearing on the broader argument about Juninho’s material legacy and Verdantine identity reconfiguration:

1. Material affordances shape dispersal and appropriation. Textiles (cloak) are prone to repair, replication, and local ritual use; metal objects (saber) are durable and attractive for institutional and diplomatic re-signification; biogenic relics are divisible and intensely personal, facilitating sacral economies. These affordances interact with institutional incentives to determine the pathways of dispersal.

2. Institutional framing alters meaning through conservation, display, and legal coding. Museums and military institutions convert vernacular artifacts into vectors of authorized national narratives (musealization), while churches and religious movements sacralize objects (relicization), and bardic networks re-embed items in performative memory practices. The same object may be remade multiple times depending on its custodian, producing layered and sometimes contradictory mythologies around Juninho.

3. Provenance gaps are political resources. Ambiguities in chains of custody have been exploited by state and foreign actors to legitimate transfers; conversely, communities and diasporas have used partial records, bardic testimony, and technical analyses to contest those transfers. The politics of evidence—what counts as proof, who may authorize analyses—becomes a site of struggle that determines whether objects shore up state narratives or enable local counter-memories.

4. Repatriation and co-curation as modalities of negotiation. Recent decades show a shift from zero-sum restitution demands to negotiated protocols that seek shared custody, community co-curation, and rotating display. These arrangements partially acknowledge the multiplicity of claims but also risk institutionalizing layered forms of appropriation unless coupled with transparent documentation and binding legal safeguards.

Concluding observation for this section
The three artifacts examined here — each materially distinct and historically entangled with different institutional actors — demonstrate how material culture operated as both medium and mechanism for the reconfiguration of Verdantine post‑war identity. Objects did not simply reflect changing narratives; they actively mediated who could claim continuity with Juninho’s legacy, on what terms, and with what public visibility. Tracing their provenance exposes the institutional logics (museal, liturgical, military, bardic) that produced durable but fragmented legacies and shows why contemporary repatriation debates and new scholarship are not purely about items in cabinets but about competing claims to memory, authority, and the right to shape national identity.

sections.name: Conclusion: Historiographical Stakes, Contemporary Reinterpretations, and Political Consequences
sections.content:
This article has followed a single, tightly bounded thread — the contested materiality of Juninho and the competing semiotic and institutional uses of his personhood — in order to draw out wider historiographical and political consequences for post‑war Verdantine life. In concluding, I set out three interrelated claims that synthesize the empirical findings and orient future work: (1) the historiographical stakes of reading Juninho materially rather than textually; (2) how contemporary reinterpretations reconfigure authority over memory; and (3) the concrete political consequences that flow from these reconfigurations.

Historiographical stakes: shifting from narrative hero to distributed artifact
Reading Juninho through the trajectories of objects and images shifts the analytic frame from heroic biography and national myth to distributed processes of institutional appropriation. This move has three implications for historiography. First, it decouples agency in memory from the individual body and relocates it in assemblages — museums, religious movements, bardic networks, and state archives — that actively produce “usable” pasts. Analytically comparable to approaches in material culture studies and lieux de mémoire, this perspective foregrounds provenance, curatorial decision-making, and performative practices (ritualization, exhibition, liturgy, anthem) as constitutive of what Juninho means at any historical moment.

Second, it problematizes unitary narratives of reconciliation that dominate official post‑war histories. The fragmented afterlives of Juninho’s objects demonstrate that reconciliation is not a singular teleology imposed by the state but a contested field where overlapping mnemonic economies — state legitimation, devotional sanctification, bardic commodification, and market commoditization — compete. This finding challenges models that privilege elite textual archives and underscores the importance of vernacular and embodied sources (oral histories, bardic repertoires, ritual protocols) for reconstructing contested pasts.

Third, methodologically, the case demonstrates the analytic value of combining provenance studies with discourse analysis and ethnography. Provenance reconstructions expose institutional transfers and legal ambiguities; iconographic and performative analyses reveal how images and objects acquire semantically dense valences; and ethnographic attention to bards and congregations shows how communities repurpose materials for ongoing moral and political ends. For historians, then, Juninho’s material afterlives are a corrective to narrative teleologies and an invitation to multi‑scalar, multimethod inquiry.

Contemporary reinterpretations: reopening claims and reconfiguring authority
Recent scholarly work, repatriation campaigns, and digital archiving efforts have reopened the contestations that were thought resolved during immediate post‑war consolidation. Three dynamics are particularly salient.

1. Repatriation and provenance politics: Renewed provenance research and public repatriation claims have exposed lacunae in museum records and in state narratives of legal transfer. These processes do not simply restore objects; they reconfigure moral authority. When a reliquary or flag is returned to a village or a bardic guild, the locus of legitimating ritual shifts, and with it the grammar of belonging and entitlement.

2. Bardic and vernacular revivals: Bardic corpora have been digitally archived and performatively reworked, generating alternative genealogies of Juninho that emphasize local grievance, poetic reparative work, or outright resistance to state commemoration. Because bards mediate affect and social memory through repetition and improvisation, their revivals produce living reinterpretations that resist museum stasis.

3. Institutional reflexivity and curatorial pluralism: Some museums and archives in Verdantine and abroad have begun to adopt collaborative exhibition models, provenance transparency, and co‑curation with claimant communities. These practices reframe museums from authoritative repositories to negotiated spaces, changing the performative effect that Juninho’s artifacts have on visitors and on civic discourse.

Political consequences: law, identity, and mobilization
The material disputes over Juninho produce tangible political effects beyond the realm of memory. Three principal consequences warrant emphasis.

1. Legal and policy implications: Provenance controversies expose inadequacies in cultural property law and transitional justice frameworks. Cases around Juninho’s remains have already pushed courts and ministerial bodies to reconceptualize thresholds for restitution, custodianship, and heritage designation. This has knock‑on effects for property regimes, municipal claims, and international heritage diplomacy.

2. Contestation of legitimacy and citizenship: Competing appropriations of Juninho — sanctified martyr, state hero, poetic ancestor — provide different groups with rhetorical resources to claim moral authority and political representation. Religious movements that sacralize Juninho base claims to social services and political legitimacy on ritual possession; bardic networks deploy his image to mobilize diasporic constituencies; the state invokes Juninho to naturalize a reconciled citizenry. These divergent deployments materially shape who is recognized as a rightful political interlocutor and how reparative goods are distributed.

3. Memory as mobilizing technology: Objects and images function as technologies of mobilization. Ritualized display, procession, and performance around Juninho’s artifacts catalyze social gatherings that can be redirected to civic advocacy or to clientelist politics. The material durability of artifacts thus enables long‑term political projects that outlast individual actors.

Toward responsible scholarship and practice
The Juninho case compels scholars and practitioners to foreground procedural ethics and plural accountability. I propose three practical orientations: (1) prioritize provenance transparency and open access to curatorial records to enable contested claims to be adjudicated on evidentiary terms; (2) institutionalize co‑curation and legal mechanisms that recognize multiple legitimate claimants (religious communities, bards, municipal bodies, diasporic kin); and (3) support living archives and performance documentation so that vernacular reinterpretations are preserved on their own terms rather than subsumed by national narratives.

Future research should deepen comparative work (placing Juninho beside similar post‑conflict figures), apply network analysis to trace object dispersals, and extend micro‑historical techniques to map the everyday politics of artifact circulation. Researchers must remain attentive to asymmetries of power — material repatriation without social reparations risks reinforcing existing hierarchies — and to the ethical stakes of representing living communities.

Conclusion
Juninho’s afterlives make clear that memory is not merely commemorative language but an infrastructural politics enacted through objects, institutions, and performances. Studying these material mediations yields a more textured account of post‑war Verdantine identity: fragmented, negotiated, and persisting through objects that continue to be fought over. The broader lesson for historians and policy‑makers is that artifacts are not inert residues of the past; they are active instruments in contemporary political life, and their custody will remain a decisive site of contestation for the foreseeable future.
